deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a set of German notes on ancient history, probably lecture or reading notes from a course on Greek and Hellenistic history. The handwriting is a rounded, schoolroom-like Kurrent and may not be Gauss's own; this needs verifying against the bundle.

It opens a new section headed 'Zweiter Zeitraum. Von dem Tode Alexanders M. bis auf die Schlacht bei Ipsus. 323 — 301', i.e. the period of the Diadochi from Alexander the Great's death (323 BC) to the battle of Ipsus (301 BC).

Content in English:
- When Alexander died, nobody knew what should happen next (the phrase 'wußte keiner' is added above the line).
- Circumstances were too complicated for anyone to form a fixed plan.
- Alexander had named no successor but had given his signet ring to Perdiccas.
- Three days after Alexander's death Perdiccas called a council to decide what should happen.
- Perdiccas at first played the modest man. He had placed a chair in place of Alexander's throne, with the ring lying on it, and then invited the assembly to choose.
- 'At first they proclaimed...' The sentence continues on fol. 138: they proclaimed him regent, he declined, then came Meleager and the proposal of Arrhidaeus.

The previous page (136) closes the first period with Alexander's death. The next page (138) continues the succession crisis and the first division of the provinces (323–321 BC).

There are no derivations, formulas or computations to reconstruct.
errors: No mathematical content, so no mathematical errors.
Historical remark on the context (previous page, not this one): the death date 'am 21 April' 323 BC is wrong. The usual dating is 10/11 June 323 BC.

Historical remark on this page: the account of the empty throne with the ring, Perdiccas's feigned modesty, Meleager and Arrhidaeus follows Curtius Rufus (Book X). The detail 'three days after his death' is not standard and may be the lecturer's or writer's own gloss; minor.

results.what: Narrative notes on the succession crisis after Alexander the Great's death (Perdiccas, the signet ring, the council at Babylon), opening a section on 323–301 BC

deep.surprise_reason: The page is routine ancient-history notes (possibly not even in Gauss's hand) with no mathematical content. Nothing here bears on the history of mathematics.
transcription_corrections: Line 5: 'was zu[?] nun[?] werden sollte' more plausibly reads 'was zunächst werden sollte'. 'wußte keiner' is a superscript insertion placed after the death cross '†'.
Line 15: 'für {+den+} Thron [-des-] Alexanders' — 'den' is inserted above the line before 'Thron'. Whether 'des' is struck is unclear; the original likely read 'für den Thron des Alexanders'.
'Conseil zu sammen' is written as two words in the manuscript ('zusammen').
'Perdiccas' is underlined both times it appears (lines 10 and 13).
